# Processes vs Threads

[Section](README.md) · [CS fundamentals](../README.md) · [Home](../../README.md)

> **In one line:** a process is an isolated address space with at least one thread; threads are units of execution that share their process's memory.

## Notes

- A **process** has its own virtual address space, file descriptors and security context. Creating one (`fork`/`CreateProcess`) is relatively expensive, and processes talk via IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory).
- A **thread** has its own stack, registers and program counter, but shares the heap, globals and open files of its process. It is cheap to create and communicates through shared memory, which **requires synchronization**.
- **Context switch:** switching threads of the same process skips the address-space switch (no TLB flush), so it is cheaper than a process switch.
- **Failure isolation:** a crashing thread takes down the whole process; a crashing process does not affect others. This is why Chrome runs a process per tab.
- **Python:** the GIL lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, so use `multiprocessing` for CPU-bound work and threads or `asyncio` for I/O-bound work.

## Trade-offs

| Option | Pros | Cons | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Multiple processes | Isolation, true parallelism in Python, crash containment | Higher memory, slower IPC | CPU-bound work, untrusted code, robustness |
| Multiple threads | Cheap, shared memory, fast communication | Races, deadlocks, one crash kills all | Shared state, parallel work in Java/C++ |
| Async (event loop) | Thousands of concurrent I/O tasks on one thread | CPU-bound work blocks everything | Network servers, I/O-bound work |

## Flashcards

The whole note is reviewed as one item: answer each card out loud before opening it.

<details><summary>Q: What do threads in the same process share, and what is private?</summary>

A: Shared: heap, globals, code, open files, the address space. Private: stack, registers, program counter, thread-local storage.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: Why is a thread context switch cheaper than a process context switch?</summary>

A: No change of address space, so there are no page-table switches or TLB flushes; only the registers and stack pointer change.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: CPU-bound task in Python: threads or processes? Why?</summary>

A: Processes. The GIL serializes Python bytecode across threads, so threads give no CPU parallelism.

</details>

<details><summary>Q: What happens to the other threads if one thread segfaults?</summary>

A: The whole process is killed, including every thread in it.

</details>
